title: Linear Transformation
body:
A **linear transformation** is a function $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ between
[[Vector Space|vector spaces]] that respects the only two operations a vector space has:

$$
T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v}), \qquad T(c\mathbf{u}) = cT(\mathbf{u})
$$

Both conditions together say **$T$ commutes with linear combinations**: transforming a
combination gives the same answer as transforming the pieces and combining afterwards. That is
the property the whole subject is named for, and it is what makes it possible to know what $T$
does everywhere from knowing what it does to a [[Basis]].

Two immediate consequences: $T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$ always, so any map that shifts the
origin is **not** linear; and a linear transformation sends lines to lines (or to a point) and
never bends anything.

Non-example worth carrying: $f(x) = mx + b$ with $b \neq 0$ is called a "linear function" in
high school and is **not** a linear transformation. It moves the origin. It is *affine*: a
linear map plus a translation.

## Every linear transformation is a matrix

This is the theorem that ties the course together. Because $T$ respects combinations, and every
$\mathbf{x}$ is a combination of the standard basis vectors:

$$
T(\mathbf{x}) = T(x_1\mathbf{e}_1 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{e}_n) = x_1T(\mathbf{e}_1) + \cdots + x_nT(\mathbf{e}_n)
$$

which is exactly $A\mathbf{x}$ for the matrix $A$ whose **columns are $T(\mathbf{e}_1), \dots,
T(\mathbf{e}_n)$**. That $A$ is the **standard matrix** of $T$.

So a [[Matrix]] and a linear transformation are the same object seen two ways: a grid of numbers,
or a map. And building the matrix is mechanical: **hit each basis vector, write down where it
lands, stack the results as columns.**

Worked, for rotation by $\theta$ in the plane. $\mathbf{e}_1 = (1,0)$ goes to $(\cos\theta,
\sin\theta)$ and $\mathbf{e}_2 = (0,1)$ goes to $(-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$, so

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}
$$

No derivation needed beyond drawing two arrows.

## The geometric operators

| Transformation | Standard matrix ($2 \times 2$) | $\det$ |
|---|---|---|
| rotation by $\theta$ | $\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$ | $1$ |
| reflection in the $x$-axis | $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ | $-1$ |
| scaling by $c$ | $\begin{bmatrix} c & 0 \\ 0 & c \end{bmatrix}$ | $c^2$ |
| horizontal shear by $k$ | $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & k \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ | $1$ |
| projection onto the $x$-axis | $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ | $0$ |

The determinant column is doing real work, exactly as [[Determinant]] describes: $1$ means area
is preserved, $-1$ means preserved but mirrored, $0$ means the map collapsed the plane onto a
line and cannot be undone.

## Composition and inverses

**Composing transformations is multiplying their matrices**: the matrix of $S \circ T$ is
$A_S A_T$, in that order. This is the reason [[Matrix Multiplication]] is defined the way it is,
and the reason it is [[Non-Commutative]]: rotate-then-reflect and reflect-then-rotate are
different maps.

$T$ is invertible exactly when its standard matrix is, and the inverse map's matrix is
$A^{-1}$. Every equivalent condition in the table in [[Matrix Inverse]] now reads as a statement
about the map: invertible means one-to-one and onto, means nothing is collapsed, means the
[[Kernel and Range|kernel]] is trivial.

Solving $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ reads, in this language, as "which input does $T$ send to
$\mathbf{b}$?" See [[System of Linear Equations]].

## Beyond $\mathbb{R}^n$

The definition only mentions addition and scalar multiplication, so it applies to any vector
space. Differentiation is a linear transformation on the space of polynomials, since
$(f+g)' = f' + g'$ and $(cf)' = cf'$; so is integration; so is the Fourier transform. **A large
part of why [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] and [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] look like linear
algebra is that they are**: the operators are linear, the functions are vectors, and
[[Orthogonal Functions]] supply the basis.

Once the space is not $\mathbb{R}^n$ the matrix depends on which [[Basis]] you picked, and
changing basis changes the matrix while leaving the transformation alone. Picking the basis that
makes the matrix diagonal is [[Diagonalization]].

## Related

- [[Matrix]] and [[Matrix Multiplication]]: the same thing, written down
- [[Kernel and Range]]: what a transformation kills and what it can reach
- [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]]: the directions $T$ leaves alone
- [[Determinant]]: how $T$ scales volume
- [[Non-Linear]] (`Books/`): a composition of these is another one of these, which is why a deep
  [[Neural Network]] with no [[Activation Function]] collapses to a single layer
